title: Mesh Independence Study in CFD: GCI Worked Example | Skill-Lync
summary: How to do a mesh independence study in CFD: three meshes, apparent order, Richardson extrapolation and the GCI, worked on our own solver's results.
body_markdown:
A mesh independence study (also called a grid independence or grid convergence study) shows that your CFD answer no longer depends on the mesh. You do one properly by solving the same case on at least three systematically refined meshes, with each cell size at least 1.3 times smaller than the last. From the three results you calculate the apparent order of accuracy, a Richardson-extrapolated value and a Grid Convergence Index (GCI), which is an error band on your finest result. "The answer changed by less than 1%" is not enough on its own.


This guide is for CFD students and junior analysts who need a mesh study that holds up in a project report, a journal paper or an interview. We wrote a small Navier-Stokes solver, ran a classic test case (the lid-driven cavity) on seven meshes and worked through the published procedure of Celik et al. (2008) line by line, using our own numbers. Because a highly accurate benchmark exists for this flow, we can also check whether the GCI band really contains the right answer.


> **In short**
>
>
> - Our four-mesh study (48 × 48 to 162 × 162 cells, refinement ratio 1.5) gives an apparent order of **p = 2.04** , matching the scheme's formal second order, and a fine-grid GCI of **0.18%** that contains the 1024 × 1024 benchmark (Marchi et al., 2009; Skill-Lync run, 24 Nov 2026).
> - Going from 96 × 96 to 108 × 108 cells changed the centre velocity by only **0.087%** , yet the true error of the 108 mesh was **0.32%** , 3.7 times larger. A small change between two close meshes is not the error.
> - With first-order upwind convection, three meshes gave a GCI of **0.007%** while the true error was **0.39%** , about 54 times larger. The warning sign: an apparent order of 5.2 from a first-order scheme.
> - Ghia et al. (1982), the cavity benchmark most students compare with, differs from the 1024-grid solution by **1.6%** in centre velocity u and **5.2%** in v. "Matches Ghia within 2%" therefore does not prove mesh independence.
> - The ASME Journal of Fluids Engineering procedure asks for three grids with refinement ratio **r > 1.3** and a safety factor of **1.25** (Celik et al., 2008). NASA's guidance uses a safety factor of **3** when only two grids are available.


## What is a mesh independence study in CFD?


A mesh independence study is a test that the quantity you report (drag, pressure drop, a velocity or a heat flux) has stopped changing with the mesh, and an estimate of how much error the mesh still leaves. You solve the same case on progressively finer meshes, watch the monitored values converge, and extrapolate to a mesh with zero cell size.


Every CFD solver replaces the governing equations with algebra on a mesh. The difference between the algebraic answer and the exact solution of the equations is the *discretisation error* . It shrinks as the cells get smaller, roughly in proportion to


h

p

h

"Mesh independent" never means zero error. It means the error is small enough for your purpose and you know roughly how big it is. Our[guide to CFD meshing](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/technical-blogs/cfd-all-about-meshing) covers mesh types and quality; this post is about proving the mesh is fine enough.

The standard recipe is the one the ASME *Journal of Fluids Engineering* published as editorial policy: Celik, Ghia, Roache and Freitas (2008), based on Richardson extrapolation and Roache's Grid Convergence Index (Roache, 1994 and 1997). ## Worked example: a lid-driven cavity on four meshes


### The problem and the solver


The lid-driven cavity is a square box of fluid whose top wall slides sideways at constant speed. At Reynolds number 100 a single large vortex fills the box, with two tiny eddies in the bottom corners. It is the first case in the OpenFOAM tutorial guide (section 2.1) and a standard test for CFD codes. We chose it because a highly accurate reference exists: Marchi, Suero and Araki (2009) solved it on a 1024 × 1024 grid with repeated Richardson extrapolation and estimate the error of their centre velocity at about

## What happens with a first-order scheme, and what is oscillatory convergence?


A first-order scheme can make a mesh study look perfect while the answer is still wrong. We switched the convection term to first-order upwind differencing and repeated the study.


On 48, 72 and 108 cells the centre velocity was −0.20912, −0.20987 and −0.20996. The last two differ by 0.04%. The GCI formula returned


p


=


5.2


and a band of 0.007%, but the true error of the 108 mesh was 0.39%, about 54 times larger. The problem is the apparent order: a first-order scheme cannot really converge at fifth order. What happened is that upwinding's numerical diffusion (an error that smears the flow) and the other discretisation errors have opposite signs. On these meshes they nearly cancel, so the error crosses zero near 48 cells (left panel of the first figure).


Adding the 162 mesh exposes it. On 72, 108 and 162 the result goes −0.20987, −0.20996, −0.20984: it moves one way, then back. Celik et al. call this *oscillatory convergence* and give a simple test: if


ε

​


/


ε

​


<


0


, the convergence is oscillatory (here the ratio is −0.72). The asymptotic check gave 0.52 instead of 1, and the benchmark was outside the GCI band again.


What to do when you see this:


- Treat an apparent order far from the formal order (here 5.2 or 0.8 for a first-order scheme) as a warning, not a bonus. Celik et al. note that agreement with the formal order is a good sign of the asymptotic range, though disagreement alone does not prove the results are bad.
- Add a finer mesh if you can. If the differences are tiny or change sign, Celik et al. recommend further refinement and reporting the percentage of points that converge in an oscillatory way. For noisy convergence they point to the least-squares version of the GCI discussed at the Lisbon verification workshops (Eça, Hoekstra and Roache).
- Check several quantities. On the same upwind meshes, v at the centre changed by 2.2% and gave


p


=


1.15


, an honest first-order signal and a 4.5% GCI that did contain the benchmark.
- Use a second-order scheme for the results you report. The JFE policy requires methods that are at least formally second order in space, and treats hybrid and power-law blending schemes as first order unless shown otherwise.

## How should y+ and inflation layers change during mesh refinement?


Refine the near-wall mesh together with the core mesh. If the inflation (prism) layers stay the same while the core gets finer, the study only measures the error away from the wall. Wall shear, heat transfer and separation, which are often the reason for the simulation, are never tested.


Geometrically similar refinement with r = 1.5 per step: first-cell height and core size are divided by r, the layer count multiplied by r and the growth rate taken to the power 1/r.


How you do it depends on the wall treatment:


- **Wall-resolved meshes** (y+ about 1, used with SST k-ω, enhanced wall treatment or transition models). Divide the first-cell height by


r


at each step, multiply the number of layers by


r


and reduce the growth rate to


g


1/


r


, as in the figure. y+ falls from 1 to 0.67 and then 0.44, which is still in the viscous sublayer, so the wall model is the same on every mesh. The Ansys Fluent User's Guide recommends near-wall meshes with y+ of about 1 for high-accuracy wall predictions, especially heat transfer.
- **Wall-function meshes.** Here you cannot scale the first cell freely. Fluent's guide warns that with wall functions you must avoid y+ below about 30, because wall shear stress and heat transfer "can and will seriously deteriorate". A mesh starting at y+ = 60 would reach 27 after two steps of 1.5. Fluent does not generally recommend wall functions, because "they do not allow a systematic refinement of the near wall grid". If you must use them, keep y+ in the valid range on all meshes and say in the report that the GCI excludes the wall-function error. Better, switch to a y+-insensitive wall treatment.


Use our[y+ calculator](https://skill-lync.com/tools/y-plus-calculator) to set the first-cell height for each mesh, and see[near-wall treatment and y+ estimation](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/technical-blogs/cfd-near-wall-treatment-and-y-estimation) for the theory behind those limits.


## Where does a mesh study fit in verification and validation (ASME V&V 20)?


A mesh study is *solution verification* : it estimates the numerical error of one simulation. It is different from *code verification* (showing the software solves its equations correctly, for example against an exact or manufactured solution) and from *validation* (comparing with experiments to measure modelling error).


ASME V&V 20-2009, the Standard for Verification and Validation in Computational Fluid Dynamics and Heat Transfer, ties them together. As summarised by NIST (Yeo, 2020), the validation comparison error is

The order matters: verify first, then validate. Without a mesh study you cannot tell whether a mismatch with experiment comes from the physics model or from the mesh, and tuning a turbulence model to cover a mesh error gives a model that fails on the next case. The JFE policy puts it bluntly: "reasonable agreement" with experimental data alone will not justify a single-grid calculation.


## What do reviewers and employers expect in a mesh independence report?


They expect enough detail to repeat the study and a clear error band on the number you rely on. A minimal report, following Celik et al. (2008) and the JFE policy, contains:


Item What to write


Method Solver and version, discretisation of each term with its formal order, boundary condition treatment


Iterative convergence Residual drop (at least three orders of magnitude) and monitor histories


Meshes Cell counts, representative h, refinement ratios, how the inflation layers and y+ changed


Results The key quantities on every mesh, in a table


Error estimate p, extrapolated value, ea, eext, GCIfine, whether convergence was monotonic or oscillatory


Decision Which mesh you used for the remaining runs and why its GCI is acceptable for the purpose


"How did you check mesh independence?" is a standard CFD interview question. A good answer names the three meshes, the refinement ratio, the quantity monitored, the apparent order and the GCI, in two or three sentences. See our[CFD interview questions](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/top-cfd-engineer-interview-questions-you-must-know) for how this fits a technical round. If you want to write a solver like the one in this post yourself, Skill-Lync's[Introduction to CFD using MATLAB and OpenFOAM](https://skill-lync.com/mechanical-engineering-courses/introduction-cfd-matlab-openfoam) starts from finite differences; the[CFD book's chapter on the stream function and vorticity](https://skill-lync.com/books/computational-fluid-dynamics#unit-17-stream-vorticity) solves the same cavity on coarser grids.


Two limits of everything above: the GCI estimates discretisation error only, not modelling error, input error or iteration error. And it is reliable only when the meshes are in the asymptotic range, which is exactly what the order check is for.


## Frequently asked questions


### How many meshes do I need for a mesh independence study?


At least three. Three meshes are the minimum that gives the apparent order p, and Celik et al. (2008) build the GCI procedure on three. A fourth mesh is worth it when you can afford it: it lets you compute p from two triplets and confirm the asymptotic range. With only two meshes, NASA's guidance uses a safety factor of 3 instead of 1.25.


### Are mesh independence, grid independence and grid convergence the same thing?


Yes, in everyday use; "mesh" and "grid" mean the same thing. Strictly, "grid convergence" is the process of approaching the zero-cell-size answer, and "grid independent" is the end state where refinement makes no practical difference. A GCI study shows both.


### What is a good GCI value?


There is no universal threshold. Compare the GCI with the accuracy the decision needs: a 2% band on drag may be fine for ranking two design options and too large for a performance guarantee. Report it and justify it rather than quoting a rule of thumb.


### Do I also need a time-step independence study?


Yes, for transient runs. Celik et al. say iterative convergence must be checked at every time step, and the JFE policy asks authors to show temporal accuracy and limited phase error. The same Richardson and GCI procedure works with the time step in place of the cell size. Keep the Courant number in mind when you refine both; see our post on the[Courant number and stability condition](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/courant-number-and-stability-condition) .


### Can I use Ghia et al. (1982) as the exact answer for my cavity validation?


Use it as a well-known reference, not as the exact answer. Ghia's values come from a 129 × 129 grid and differ from the 1024 × 1024 extrapolated solution of Marchi et al. (2009) by 1.6% in the centre value of u and 5.2% in v at Re = 100. For a precise check, compare with Marchi et al. (2009) or the spectral solution of Botella and Peyret (1998), which covers Re = 100 and 1000.
